briefing.question: When is force just, and who gets to decide?
briefing.agreed: Force needs a real wrong and aims at peace; defense against attack is legitimate.
briefing.split: Augustine, Aquinas weigh cause and intent; Kant, Madison want the legislature to decide; Hamilton backs a fast executive; Cicero asks if talks came first.

briefing.question: Should the state serve the people's elected will or neutral expertise?
briefing.agreed: Officials answer to elected leaders; no one defended a self-ruling bureaucracy.
briefing.split: Mill, Weber, Hamilton back merit and reject political tests; Rousseau: agents of the people, not a party; Tocqueville distrusts spoils and central expertise.

briefing.question: Can you do good by speaking falsely about evil?
briefing.agreed: False praise of evil is not good in itself; courtesy is not flattery.
briefing.split: Augustine and Kant forbid the lie outright; Aquinas grades it by what it endorses; Cicero denies a dishonorable gain; Machiavelli counts its cost.

briefing.question: Conscience or law, and who owns the land?
briefing.agreed: Justice of a rule turns on facts as well as principle; accepting the penalty is honorable.
briefing.split: Thoreau and King put conscience first; Aquinas fears disorder; Socrates and Hobbes guard the law; Locke cannot settle the facts.

briefing.question: What makes a punishment just?
briefing.agreed: A penalty must track real, proven harm and actually bite.
briefing.split: Beccaria stresses certainty, Bentham a penalty above the gain; Kant desert alone; Smith distrusts punishers who profit; Brandeis prefers limits before harm.

briefing.question: Does art's purpose excuse its means?
briefing.agreed: Intent alone does not settle it; effect and target matter.
briefing.split: Aristophanes and Erasmus defend satire within limits; Plato and Tolstoy judge by what audiences absorb; Swift owns misreadings; Aristotle asks if it wounds.

briefing.question: Where does the family's authority end and the state's begin?
briefing.agreed: The state must act against real abuse; parental authority is a trust for the child.
briefing.split: Mill gives the state the widest duty; Leo XIII and Pius XI hold the family prior; Burke and Locke defend ordinary affection.

briefing.question: Is any truth too sacred to debate?
briefing.agreed: The record of the schools is not up for denial; staging matters.
briefing.split: Mill, Milton, and Popper would forbid no question; Newman faults the staging; Burke defends reverence for memory.

briefing.question: How do faith and politics relate?
briefing.agreed: No party is the kingdom of God; conscience is formed by moral truth, not party.
briefing.split: John Paul II and Calvin hold some claims fixed and grave; Augustine and Kuyper stress the pilgrim church; Locke bars coercion by church or state.

briefing.question: Justice versus mercy, and what punishment does to the society that carries it out
briefing.agreed: Execution as spectacle, cruelty, or unequal practice is indefensible.
briefing.split: Beccaria denies the right to kill; Kant holds death owed for murder; Aquinas cites the common good; Augustine pleads mercy; Mill trusts fallible tests.

briefing.question: What makes a people one?
briefing.agreed: Ancestry alone does not make a people.
briefing.split: Burke and Eliot want a lived spiritual inheritance; Augustine grounds a people in shared loves; Renan, Locke, and Rawls look to consent.

briefing.question: Is faith handed on by truth or by encounter?
briefing.agreed: Truth and encounter are not rivals; faith has content and aims at love.
briefing.split: Aquinas and Newman put doctrine first; Augustine joins story to love; Pascal and à Kempis stress the heart and an amended life.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine and Aquinas framed the just-war conditions both camps in the report appeal to: authority, cause, and intention. Cicero is the Roman source behind the idea of force as a last resort. Kant wrote a whole treatise on which constitutions make war less likely. Hamilton and Madison wrote the Federalist papers that divided war powers between Congress and the President. Vegetius, whom the hawks cite, does not get a chair, because his military manual doesn't argue the moral question.

chairs.name: Augustine
works: The City of God, Book XIX

turn.text: I never praised war. It belongs to the misery of the earthly city. In the City of God I answered those who make just war sound simple: “But, say they, the wise man will wage just wars. As if he would not all the rather lament the necessity of just wars, if he remembers that he is a man” (City of God XIX.7). Even a just war is forced on us by another's wrongdoing, and it should grieve the one who wages it.

turn.text: If you ask what is truly evil in war, it isn't chiefly that people die, since all of us will die. “The real evils in war are love of violence, revengeful cruelty, fierce and implacable enmity, wild resistance, and the lust of power, and such like” (Reply to Faustus XXII.74). Before any campaign, then, I would ask what it loves. Is it aimed at restraining violence and restoring peace, or at domination? I also held that the power to undertake war belongs to those who rightly hold public authority, not to private zeal (Reply to Faustus XXII.75, paraphrased).

turn.text: I gathered Augustine's scattered judgments into a single article. “In order for a war to be just, three things are necessary. First, the authority of the sovereign by whose command the war is to be waged.” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 40, Art. 1) The second is a just cause, meaning the other side deserves to be attacked for some fault. The third is a right intention, the advancement of good or the avoidance of evil. Those who have charge of the common weal may defend it against external enemies, just as they punish evildoers within. So the hawks are right that defending allies and shipping can be a just cause.

turn.text: But the three conditions are not a menu. I wrote that “it may happen that the war is declared by the legitimate authority, and for a just cause, and yet be rendered unlawful through a wicked intention” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 40, Art. 1). A strong grievance doesn't cure a defect of authority, and a lawful order doesn't cure cruelty or a lust for gain. I named the sovereign as the one who decides. I did not settle how a republic with divided powers names its sovereign. That question belongs to the next chairs.

A war can still be wrong if it is driven by bad motives, and he leaves open who counts as the sovereign in a modern republic.

turn.text: Before either of the bishops, I wrote that disputes can be settled in two ways: by discussion, which is proper to human beings, or by force, which is proper to beasts. So “we must resort to force only in case we may not avail ourselves of discussion” (De Officiis I.xi.34). “The only excuse, therefore, for going to war is that we may live in peace unharmed” (De Officiis I.xi.35). The skeptics' test of last resort is my rule restated.

turn.text: I would add something to Aquinas's account of authority: form matters. Rome held that “no war is just, unless it is entered upon after an official demand for satisfaction has been submitted or warning has been given and a formal declaration made” (De Officiis I.xi.36). A war begun without warning, demand, or declaration was suspect to us even when the cause was good. I also want the hawks to remember that a threat of force has to be honest to work. Rome kept its word even to enemies, and a threat made only for show teaches the other side to ignore us.

turn.text: Aquinas leaves open the question of who decides, and I put it at the center. In a republic, “If, as must be so under this constitution, the consent of the subjects is required to determine whether there shall be war or not, nothing is more natural than that they should weigh the matter well, before undertaking such a bad business.” (Perpetual Peace, First Definitive Article) The people who decide are the people who fight, pay, and repair the ruin. A ruler who owns the state and loses nothing by war is different: “He can therefore decide on war for the most trifling reasons, as if it were a kind of pleasure party.” (Perpetual Peace, First Definitive Article)

turn.text: But I part with Kant's hope that popular consent makes a nation peaceful. I asked: “Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies?” (Federalist No. 6) Assemblies feel rage, resentment, and jealousy too. I also argued that the executive needs energy, which means decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch (Federalist No. 70, paraphrased). When ships are being struck, the commander must be able to repel attack without waiting. Declaring a new war is another matter, and that belongs to the legislature.

sittings.question: What makes a people one?

setup.text: Reform UK MP Danny Kruger argued that Britain is united by commitment to the nation and its Christian foundations, not by ethnicity; some in his party countered that ancestry matters. A Theos report finds only a minority think being truly British requires being Christian.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Renan's 1882 lecture What Is a Nation? is the classic answer to exactly this question. Burke's partnership between generations and T. S. Eliot's The Idea of a Christian Society are both named in the report. Augustine defined a people by its shared loves. Locke grounds political community in consent. Rawls explains how a society divided by faith can still share a political conception. The MPs in the story are context, not chairs.

opening.text: What makes a people one? One side says a nation needs a shared moral and spiritual inheritance, and that Christianity gave Britain its ideas of law and dignity. Critics come from two directions: ethnic nationalists who say kinship matters, and pluralists and many Christians who warn that faith used as an identity badge gets emptied of belief. The report adds “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.” (Matthew 22:21) Renan, please begin.
